home.intro: park.fan shows live wait times and crowd levels for more than 200 theme parks and nearly 7,000 attractions worldwide, among them the Disney and Universal parks, Europa-Park and Phantasialand. It also has opening hours and its own forecast for the days ahead.

hero.title: Where is the wait worth it today?

ai.title: How accurate our forecasts are
ai.subtitle: park.fan runs a model of its own, trained on the queues measured at more than 200 parks. It factors in the weather forecast, school holidays and special events, and every day at 06:00 UTC it learns from the previous day’s wait times.
ai.avgErrorDesc: MAE: how many minutes off our predictions are on average
ai.rmseDesc: RMSE: how bad the worst misses are, outliers weighted more
ai.mapeDesc: MAPE: percentage error relative to actual wait time
ai.coverageDesc: of all predictions checked against measurements
ai.r2ScoreDesc: R²: how well the model explains wait time variance
ai.howText: Three things go into every forecast: the park’s measured wait-time history; the weather forecast, school holidays and public holidays; and what is happening at the park that day, such as a special event or the start of the season. From those the model works out the expected wait per ride and per hour and combines them into the day’s crowd level, as far ahead as the park has published its schedule.
ai.fancastLink: How Fancast, our forecasting model, works
ai.improvingTitle: Every forecast is checked the day after
ai.improvingText: The day after a forecast, the system lays it next to the wait time actually measured and writes the difference into the next training run. The figures above come from that comparison.

steps.title: Planning a park day
steps.lead: Pick a park, check the day, then decide what order to ride in. For each of the three steps, park.fan has measurements from more than 200 parks.

one.title: Pick a park
one.text: Type the park or the ride, or take the suggestion near you. Every park has its own page with live wait times, opening hours and a calendar.
one.tip: The search also finds rides, shows and restaurants. Type “Taron” and you get the ride along with its park.
one.label: Search for a park or ride

two.title: Check the day
two.text: The crowd calendar gives every day a colour, as far ahead as the park has published its schedule. Green means as busy as usual or quieter, red means much busier than a typical day at that park.
two.tip: Days next to each other often have different colours. If you can move your date, look at the week before and the week after as well before you book.
two.caption: A month in the calendar: one tile per day, the colour is the crowd level expected.

three.title: Plan the route
three.text: Every ride has a curve for the day, built from the days it was measured. On it you can see what time of day the queue is usually shortest.
three.tip: The curve is a median over many days. If a ride breaks down in the morning, the rest of that day will look different from the curve.
three.caption: A coaster’s typical day, from opening to evening.
three.best: The quietest windows sit early and in the last hour.

nearby.title: Theme parks near you
nearby.lead: With your location, park.fan lists the nearest parks, open ones first, and shows how busy each one is right now.

live.title: Wait times for every ride, refreshed every five minutes
live.lead: For every attraction and every queue type, plus opening hours and breakdowns.
live.body: 95 minutes is a lot on a Tuesday in September and an ordinary morning on a Saturday in October. That’s why every ride page lists the typical wait for that weekday and how long the queue gets on busy days.
live.ridesTitle: Every ride has its own page
live.ridesText: A ride’s page lists its queue types, its day as measured and as forecast, typical wait times by weekday, the height limit and a rope-drop tip.
live.ropeDropText: Head here as soon as the park opens. On the popular rides the first hour is usually the quietest of the day.
live.howtoLink: Guide to reading and judging wait times

shows.title: When the show starts and where to eat
shows.lead: For each park, park.fan lists the shows with their times and the restaurants with their cuisine, opening hours and whether booking is required.
shows.showsHint: Every performance of the day with its time, the next one first, and whether the show is currently in season.
shows.restaurantsHint: Cuisine, opening hours and whether you need to book a table.
shows.body: While a big show is running, its audience is not queueing anywhere. When it ends, they all come back at once. The show times let you ride something while the show is on.

calendar.title: A green day or a red one?
calendar.lead: The calendar rates every day the park has already published opening hours for. Look at it before you book a hotel.
calendar.pipelineTitle: How a day gets its colour
calendar.pipelineLead: Four steps, run again every night.

p1.title: Measure
p1.text: Every five minutes park.fan polls the parks’ queue systems: standby, single rider, Lightning Lane, virtual queues, plus the operating status of every ride.
p1.label: Measurement interval

p2.title: Collect
p2.text: Every reading is stored with its timestamp, ride and park. From them you can follow how each ride’s wait time changes over a day, a week and a season.
p2.label: Records

p3.title: Enrich
p3.text: Signals from outside join in: the weather forecast, school and public holidays from the countries the parks stand in, bridge days, and special events like Halloween or the start of the season.
p3.label: Holidays, weather

p4.title: Forecast
p4.text: Fancast turns all of that into an expected wait per ride and per hour, then condenses it into the day’s crowd level, which is the colour you see in the calendar.
p4.label: Days ahead

calendar.feedback: The next day every forecast is laid against the wait time actually measured. The difference goes into the next round of training, and that is why the calendar colour for one and the same day changes as the day gets closer.
calendar.body: The colour compares the day with a typical day at the same park. Green means as busy as usual or quieter, orange and red mean longer queues than usual. So a red day at a small park can still mean shorter waits than a green day at Europa-Park.
calendar.bestTimeLink: Best time to visit: the quietest weekdays and months

ai.title: A forecast of our own, with the error printed next to it
ai.lead: The forecasts come from Fancast, a model park.fan trains itself. It is retrained every day at 06:00 UTC on the previous day’s wait times.
ai.compareLead: Three approaches are common. None of them publishes how far off its forecasts turned out to be.

c1.title: No forecast at all
c1.text: One of the best-known German wait-time sites deliberately does without predictions: too many factors, and a wrong forecast could hurt parks and visitors alike. All it shows is how busy it was.
c1.limit: From a look back you can’t work out which day next month will be busy.

c2.title: The average of similar days
c2.text: A statistical model looks for comparable days in the past (same weekday, same holiday situation) and averages them. Usually 90 days ahead and often for a single park only.
c2.limit: Without three comparable days the day stays empty.

c3.title: Statistics plus a bit of AI
c3.text: Ensembles mix statistical analysis with an AI share and factor in holidays and weather, labelled beta, for one park, in steps from “excellent” to “very long”.
c3.limit: There is no figure for how often the level is right.

ai.answerTitle: Fancast forecasts by the hour, ride by ride, and publishes its error.
ai.answerText: Alongside the day’s crowd level, every ride gets an expected wait for each hour. Each forecast is later compared with what was actually measured, and the accuracy figures further down come from that comparison.

bestTime.title: Many rides have two quiet windows, in the morning and towards the evening
bestTime.lead: Rope drop does not help on every ride. Some are equally busy all day, others only fill up from midday. The curve is one ride’s median across its measured days.
bestTime.chartSubtitle: Median of {days} measured days, sampled every 5 minutes
bestTime.heatText: On hot days more people queue for the water rides. That is why the weather forecast goes into the calendar.
bestTime.historyText: The model works out each ride separately, from that ride’s own day curve and season. Whatever is measured today goes into training the next morning.
bestTime.hubLink: Best time to visit for 200+ parks
bestTime.windowClosing: Towards the end of the day

inPark.title: Favourites and the park map for the day of your visit
inPark.lead: Before your visit you plan with the calendar and the forecast. In the park you are more likely to check the rides you saved and the park map with its wait times.
inPark.favText: Tap the star and the park or ride shows up on your homepage, with its live wait time and opening status. Favourites are saved in your browser and need no account.
inPark.mapText: Rides, shows and restaurants appear on the park map as coloured markers. Tap one to see its status and wait time. When you’re in the park, your position is marked on the map and the nearest rides move to the top.

dictionary.title: Track elements such as the zero-G roll and the Immelmann in the 3-D player
dictionary.lead: The dictionary explains terms like airtime, rope drop and single rider. You can play track elements in the 3-D player and stop them at any point of the ride.

r1.title: Our own model, trained daily
r1.text: Fancast was built at park.fan, from the data preparation to the training, and is retrained every morning on the previous day’s wait times.

r2.title: The accuracy is published
r2.text: The mean error and the R² value are on this page and are recalculated after every training run, even when they get worse.

r3.title: New wait times every five minutes
r3.text: park.fan reads three public sources and checks them against each other. When a ride goes down, it’s marked on its page with the next update.

r4.title: Free, no account needed
r4.text: There is no paywall and no subscription tier with more data. Everything park.fan has on a park is on that park’s page for anyone to see.

r5.title: 200+ parks, 23 countries, 6 languages
r5.text: Tokyo DisneySea, Efteling and Phantasialand are among them. Where a park publishes its wait times, they are here; where it doesn’t, there’s a note on the park page.

r6.title: Articles with measured data
r6.text: The blog has park guides and analyses, for example of why a park is packed in October and nearly empty in November. The wait times in those articles are live widgets that load the current figures.

founder.title: A developer who queued once too often
founder.name: Patrick Arns
founder.p1: park.fan is run by one person, Patrick, who has been going to theme parks since he was a child and has been a software developer for more than 25 years. It began with 90 minutes in the queue for a single ride, and the feeling that a little planning would have avoided it.
founder.p2: That turned into a wait-time tracker, then a database, and finally the forecasting model, which is retrained every day. He built the data import, the model and this website himself.
founder.authorLink: More about Patrick on the blog

method.title: Where these numbers come from
method.measured: Every figure on this page comes from measurements. The source is the <posted>posted wait time</posted> published {inPark}: park.fan reads it continuously and files every reading with a timestamp. This analysis covers {days} operating days across {years} years.
method.percentiles: “Typical” is the median of all readings: half the <wait>wait times</wait> were below it, half above. “Peak” is the 90th percentile, the value only one reading in ten went past. The median is what to expect, the peak is what a full day looks like. A month’s <crowd>crowd level</crowd> sums up both across every ride.
method.hourly: The day curve rests on a shorter window: {days} operating days since {from}. Hours in which a ride reported nothing stay empty and don’t count as zero minutes.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.waitTimesQ: What are the wait times at {park} today?
faq.waitTimesA: Right now the average wait at {park} is about {avg} minutes (peak {peak} minutes) across {operating} open attractions. Live wait times for every ride are shown above on this page.
faq.waitTimesNoDataA: Wait times at {park} vary by day and season. The live wait times for every ride are above, and the crowd calendar has the best time to visit.
faq.openingHoursQ: What are the opening hours for {park} today?
faq.openingHoursEvergreenA: Opening hours at {park} vary by season and day. Check the schedule and crowd calendar on this page for the current opening times.
faq.diningQ: What dining options are available at {park}?
faq.crowdCalendarA: Yes. The crowd calendar {forPark} rates every single day, and for parks that open year-round it reaches up to a year ahead. Green days mean short queues, red ones long.
faq.leastCrowdedA: {park} is typically quietest on {days}. The next quiet days are in the <calendar>crowd calendar</calendar> above.
faq.leastCrowdedNoDataA: Check the <calendar>crowd calendar</calendar> on this page for upcoming quiet days. Green days signal short queues and smaller crowds.

attraction.title: Frequently Asked Questions
attraction.waitTimeQ: How long is the wait for {attraction}?
attraction.waitTimeA: Wait times for {attraction} vary by day and season. Check live wait times on park.fan.
attraction.waitTimeStatsA: Today the wait for {attraction} averages {avg} minutes, ranging from {min} to {max} minutes. The current live wait time is shown above on this page.
attraction.singleRiderQ: Does {attraction} have a Single Rider line?
attraction.singleRiderA: Yes. If you ride alone, you can use the single rider line at {attraction} and fill an empty seat.
attraction.paidQueueQ: Is there a fast pass option for {attraction}?
attraction.paidQueueA: Yes, expedited access is available via {type}.

faq.whatIsA: park.fan collects live wait times from more than 200 theme parks in 23 countries. Every park page carries the current wait time for every ride, the show times, the opening hours and a calendar that rates the crowds for the months ahead.
faq.whichParksQ: Which theme parks are supported by park.fan?
faq.whichParksA: park.fan covers over 200 theme parks worldwide, among them Phantasialand, Europa-Park, Disneyland Paris, Efteling, Walibi Belgium, Toverland and Bobbejaanland. The full list with live wait times is on the parks overview page.
faq.liveDataQ: Are the wait times on park.fan live and in real-time?
faq.liveDataA: Yes. Wherever a park publishes its wait times, we poll them every five minutes from three public sources at once: ThemeParks.wiki, Wartezeiten.app and Queue-Times.com. Where the sources disagree, the majority decides, then the median, then the mean. The result is rounded to five minutes, because that is how the parks post them.
faq.freeA: Yes. Live wait times, opening hours, shows, restaurants and the crowd calendar are all there without an account and without a paywall. There is no subscription tier with more data behind it.
faq.favoritesQ: Can I save my favorite parks and attractions on park.fan?
faq.favoritesA: Yes. Tap the star on a park, a ride, a show or a restaurant. Your favorites then appear on the homepage with their live wait time and opening status. They are saved in your browser, and you do not need an account.
faq.featuresQ: What information does park.fan offer besides live wait times?
faq.featuresA: Every park page also carries the opening hours, the show times, the restaurants with their cuisine and whether a table has to be booked, the day’s weather forecast, the measured wait-time history and the crowd calendar. Each ride’s own page adds the typical course of its day.
faq.mobileA: Yes. park.fan runs in the browser on a phone, a tablet or a computer, so there is no app to install. In the park you can use it to see where the queue is short right now. When the site can tell you are inside a park, the nearest rides move to the top.

news.metaTitle: Theme park news: events, openings and dates

news.intro: What is happening at the parks, newest first.

howto.tagline: 70 minutes at Taron: a lot, or normal? You can only tell once it’s set against the days park.fan has already measured at Taron.

fancast.tagline: It reads millions of live wait times to predict how busy a park will be on every day it has published. The next day, every forecast is checked against the measured wait, and the average error in minutes is published on this page.

next.title: Your date in the crowd calendar
next.body: On every park page each published day is green, yellow or red, with the region’s school holidays and public holidays counted in.

bestTime.tagline: Theme-park crowds follow a pattern. From the wait times we’ve measured at 200+ parks since December 2025, here are the quietest days and how to dodge the busy ones.

next.title: Found your day?
next.body: In the trip planner you pick the rides you want, and the forecast waits show whether they all fit in before the park closes. How well the crowd calendar’s forecasts did over the last 30 days is on the Fancast page.

next.title: No date yet?
next.body: The quietest weekdays and months from wait times measured at over 200 parks, and on every park page a crowd calendar with a forecast for each day the park has published.
